When the meltdown comes out of nowhere

By CJ LimAutism Educator & Founder of APC

Reviewed 17 September 2026

One minute your child seems okay. The next, they are screaming, hitting or unable to respond. When you cannot see what changed, deciding what to do can feel just as difficult as the moment itself.

In this guide
  • Look beyond the last thing that happened
  • A response to adapt to your child
  • Try, notice and adjust
  • When to seek more support

Look beyond the last thing that happened

A meltdown describes intense overwhelm. Noise, uncertainty, pain, tiredness or several demands together may contribute. The last request you made may be only part of the picture. You cannot reliably work out the cause from the outward behaviour alone, and not every upset has the same explanation.

During intense distress, start with safety and reducing pressure. Save questions about what happened for a time when your child can engage.

A response to adapt to your child

1

Make the space safer

Move hazards away and give other people space. If moving your child would add distress, consider whether you can make the current space quieter instead. Use an agreed safety plan if your family has one.

2

Reduce what you can

Pause non-essential instructions, lower your voice and reduce noise or bright light where possible. Use a few familiar words, such as “I am here.” Your child may still need clear, brief information about immediate safety.

3

Offer space without disappearing

Some children want a trusted adult nearby; others need more distance. Do not assume a hug will help. Watch their response and keep supervision appropriate to their age and safety needs.

4

Allow recovery before a conversation

Offer a familiar drink, place or activity when your child is ready. A debrief can wait. Later, invite their account through speech, pictures, writing or another communication method they use.

Keep reading at your own pace. Explore a related guide, or use APC Calm for short prompts around routines, transitions and communication.

Sharing a plan with school

Ask what staff notice before distress, where your child can take a break and how they can request help. Share responses your child accepts at home, but expect to adapt them to the school setting. Agree how adults will record concerns and contact you.

Try, notice and adjust

After a difficult moment, make a short note of what happened beforehand, what you observed and what followed. Include possible pain, sleep changes and your child's own account. Choose one manageable adjustment to review, such as a quieter transition. No clear pattern is also useful information; it does not mean you missed something obvious.

When to seek more support

Seek professional advice if distress is new, increasing, frequent or involves injury. A doctor can assess possible health contributors. If there is immediate serious danger, seek emergency help. General parent guidance is not a substitute for an individual safety assessment.

Sources and further reading

  • National Autistic Society: meltdowns
  • NICE: supporting autistic children and young people

These sources inform the general guidance. The everyday examples are suggestions to adapt to your child, not an individual assessment or treatment plan.
